metadata.title: TMUA 2017 · Paper 2
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Expands a squared numerator over a radical denominator and differentiates the resulting powers; adds a gradient evaluation.
The same radical-quotient simplification exposes a short power-rule calculation.
Another radical denominator gives positive and negative fractional powers whose derivative signs must be retained.
Uses a perpendicular line and its axis intercept, adding the midpoint condition of a perpendicular bisector.
Finds the height where perpendicular lines meet and uses it in an area calculation, transferring the same gradient-to-geometry chain.

Both use perpendicular geometry to recover coordinate-related lengths. The candidate uses a tangent-radius right angle and similar triangles to obtain an axis intercept, transferring the original right-triangle reasoning without repeating its slope calculation.
Uses a convergent GP together with an AP condition, requiring the ratio and convergence restriction to survive the algebra.
Eliminates an AP difference to relate GP terms and sums. It extends translating term positions into powers of a common ratio.

Both derive or use a GP ratio, enforce convergence and apply the infinite-sum formula. Only the candidate adds a strict sum threshold and probability over integer parameters; the original asks for one exact infinite sum.
Uses an angle’s quadrant together with a trigonometric ratio, preventing a correct-looking value obtained from the wrong branch.
Reduces a trigonometric condition then uses the final quadrant to determine the correct sign.
Directly checks the required true-hypothesis, false-conclusion structure for proposed counterexamples.
Requires checking the digit-pattern hypothesis before a composite number can refute a primality claim.
Separates eligible counterexamples from examples failing the hypothesis or satisfying the conclusion.
Evaluates an integral-defined numerical term before summing the resulting sequence, reinforcing that a definite integral produces a number.
Repeated square rooting becomes repeated halving of an exponent. It practises converting a repeated operation into a simple sequence rule.
sharedKnowledge: convert a repeated operation to a numerical recurrence

matches.rationale: Shows how a simple differentiation-and-multiplication operation acts as a constant factor on a power. This is an operator-to-algebra transfer, not another integral recurrence.
sharedKnowledge: convert a calculus operation into an algebraic multiplier

matches.rationale: Recognises an exponential-function graph from limits and monotonicity instead of a vague visual resemblance.
Uses exact points and direction to identify a variable-base logarithm, reinforcing the relationship between base and exponent.
Linearises nested logarithms and identifies a crossover before ordering the functions; it extends same-input graph comparisons.
Compares a mixed set of exact trigonometric, logarithmic and radical quantities without a calculator.

Prerequisite transfer: both simplify positive surd expressions exactly and check signs before cancelling or taking reciprocals. The nested-square candidate concentrates on recognizing binomial squares; the mixed-expression problem additionally compares several kinds of number against a common benchmark.
Proves which exponential inequality must hold by comparing ordered exponents; this extends numerical bounding to a universal statement.

Both require finding the first unsupported line of a proof. The original assumes equality of corresponding factors, while the candidate mishandles subtraction of a bracket; it practises the ordered proof-audit discipline using a different algebraic operation.
sharedKnowledge: Distinguish later consequences from the first error

matches.rationale: The original wrongly matches corresponding factors of equal products; the follow-up replaces a signed trigonometric quantity by its principal square root. Both require finding the first unjustified deduction, but the different factor and sign operations make this a prerequisite transfer.
sharedKnowledge: Audit each operation under its stated assumptions

matches.rationale: The original tests an unjustified equality of corresponding factors; the candidate loses a solution through division by a possibly zero expression. Both require auditing equivalence in order, but the algebraic failure is different.
sharedKnowledge: Check each inference against the original domain
Identify the first loss of equivalence

matches.rationale: Tests which symmetry conditions guarantee equal integrals and rejects unsupported necessity claims.
Uses input reflection while separating signed and absolute integrals, strengthening the geometric interpretation of cancellation.

Both use cancellation of equal-width opposite signed areas and assess what guarantees a zero integral. The candidate derives the exact condition from complete sine periods and partial-period signs; the original starts from a symmetry identity about the midpoint. No trigonometric antiderivative is needed.
sharedKnowledge: Both use cancellation of equal-width opposite signed areas and assess what guarantees a zero integral. The candidate derives the exact condition from complete sine periods and partial-period signs; the original starts from a symmetry identity about the midpoint. No trigonometric antiderivative is needed.

matches.rationale: A translated graph changes limits and adds the rectangular area from a constant vertical shift.
Combines overlapping signed integrals to recover geometric lobe areas; it specifically trains the sign check needed before using an area as an integral.

Both partition the permitted angular domain using trigonometric zeros and preserve signs under doubled inputs. The candidate isolates this interval-sign prerequisite by assembling negative-product intervals; it does not compare all three original curve orderings.

Both compare trigonometric graph landmarks on a specified interval using exact values and endpoint behaviour. The candidate identifies variable-power curves, rather than proving a simultaneous ordering of three original curves impossible.
Turns numerical representation information into allowed measurement intervals, then chooses the correct bound. It covers precision rather than standard-form carries.
Combines given inequalities to prove forced comparisons and uses a permitted counterexample to reject an unjustified inference.
Recovers a quadratic using its vertex and a point, reinforcing the meaning of completed-square parameters.
Tracks a vertex under horizontal scaling and translation to identify the correct transformed graph.
Expresses a parameter-dependent vertex height and then minimises it, extending the same square-completion comparison.
Computes a short recurrence cycle and groups complete pairs to avoid evaluating many terms.
sharedKnowledge: align the initial term and group full blocks

matches.rationale: Finds and verifies a four-cycle in a rational recurrence before locating a large indexed term.
sharedKnowledge: Align the first term with the cycle

matches.rationale: Tracks partial sums across a six-term cycle, keeping the block position and any remaining terms aligned.
Chooses a function satisfying a derivative condition everywhere but violating a value claim somewhere, matching the all-input premise and one-input failure structure.
Uses a valid integer example to separate divisibility necessity from sufficiency. This strengthens the integer-premise side of the original counterexample.
sharedKnowledge: one eligible counterexample to a universal claim

matches.rationale: Both test whether a whole-function premise is preserved by differentiation. A candidate polynomial must satisfy the premise over its complete domain before a derivative value can refute the conclusion. The original premise is integer-valuedness; the candidate changes it to pointwise height ordering and adds integral claims.
sharedKnowledge: Both test whether a whole-function premise is preserved by differentiation. A candidate polynomial must satisfy the premise over its complete domain before a derivative value can refute the conclusion. The original premise is integer-valuedness; the candidate changes it to pointwise height ordering and adds integral claims.

matches.rationale: Negates a definition involving every eligible factor and some member of a set, retaining both divisibility direction and domains.

Distinguishes universal from existential choices and preserves which later choices may depend on earlier inputs. This transfers the original scope-reading prerequisite from a nested divisibility definition to real and integer witnesses.
Negates every–some–every in order and then negates the final primality property.
Rewrites different exponential bases as powers of one base. This isolates the exponent-comparison prerequisite without a proof-auditing layer.
Tracks order reversals when multiplying or dividing by negative quantities, reinforcing why a direction change needs justification.
Rejects invalid operations on simultaneous inequalities and tests the exact sign conditions needed for a step to be valid.
Uses polynomial end behaviour and extrema counts to reject an impossible maximum/minimum configuration.

Both differentiate polynomials and compare turning heights with the axis to check a claimed relation between stationary inputs and distinct roots. The candidate tests both implication directions with freely chosen polynomials; the original has a fixed cubic family and offered parameter subsets.
sharedKnowledge: Both differentiate polynomials and compare turning heights with the axis to check a claimed relation between stationary inputs and distinct roots. The candidate tests both implication directions with freely chosen polynomials; the original has a fixed cubic family and offered parameter subsets.

matches.rationale: Both compute polynomial derivatives and count their real zeros separately from zeros of the original polynomial. The candidate isolates that distinction through constructive examples and also multiplies the derivative by x; it does not practise the original turning-height parameter inequalities.
sharedKnowledge: Both compute polynomial derivatives and count their real zeros separately from zeros of the original polynomial. The candidate isolates that distinction through constructive examples and also multiplies the derivative by x; it does not practise the original turning-height parameter inequalities.

matches.rationale: Both enumerate complete permutations subject to position or relative-order restrictions. The runner question fixes forced positions and counts orders; the password question first enumerates excluded-position assignments, then additionally designs distinguishing feedback. Only the constrained-permutation enumeration is shared.
sharedKnowledge: Both enumerate complete permutations subject to position or relative-order restrictions. The runner question fixes forced positions and counts orders; the password question first enumerates excluded-position assignments, then additionally designs distinguishing feedback. Only the constrained-permutation enumeration is shared.

review.source: Official papers and official worked answers, with question-specific reviewed links
scopeNotes: The archive has only one standard-form carry question. Q13 follow-ups train translating representation into bounds and testing must-be-true claims.
The password one-query problem has no exact archive duplicate. Q20 follow-ups train the complete-case and constrained-permutation prerequisites.
For Q12 the explanation follows the official graph-based approach using the supplied curves and a standard tangent sketch; no double-angle identity is assumed.
